analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal board to flag overpriced prescription drugs and revoke patents when drugmakers refuse to cut prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in a House subcommittee for the rest of the two-year Congress after being referred on April 14, 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set up a five-member Prescription Drug Price Review Board, whose members could not have worked for a drugmaker in the previous three years. The board would review the price of every prescription drug, decide whether the price or a price increase was excessive using factors like what the drug sells for abroad and how much of its research the government paid for, and publish plain-language guides so consumers could compare prices. If a manufacturer refused to lower a price the board found excessive after a public hearing, the board could revoke the drug's patent — allowing competitors to make the drug.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who pay for prescription drugs — especially seniors on Medicare, which did not cover outpatient prescription drugs at the time, and uninsured people paying full price. Consumers would gain both from price reviews that pressured drugmakers to lower prices and from a published consumer's guide to drug prices. Taxpayers would gain where federally funded research produced drugs later sold at high prices, since the board would factor the government's share of research costs into its review.

how_it_helps.text: The board would review the price of every prescription drug on the market and every new drug, using data including ten years of U.S. and foreign wholesale prices, manufacturing costs, and the share of research costs paid by U.S. taxpayers [S3].

If the board found a price excessive after a public hearing and the manufacturer refused to reduce it, the board could revoke the drug's patent, opening the door to cheaper generic competition [S2] [S3].
The board would publish an easy-to-understand annual consumer's guide to prescription drug prices and inform consumers about price increases by manufacturer and drug class [S3].

The bill directed a study by the Institute of Medicine on making prescription drugs affordable, including whether Medicare should reimburse for prescription drugs at prices negotiated with manufacturers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose prices would be subject to government review and who could lose a patent — their most valuable asset — if they refused to lower a price the board found excessive. Consumers might also pay indirectly if slower expected returns led manufacturers to develop fewer new drugs.

drawbacks.text: Revoking a patent is an unusually severe penalty: a patent is the legal foundation of a drug company's returns, and revoking it as a pricing sanction could be challenged as a taking and would risk diverting investment away from developing new medicines [S3].

Price caps can reduce the revenue that funds research into new drugs; the bill itself acknowledged this trade-off by ordering a study of which federal incentives best encourage development of low-cost, effective drugs [S3].

Comparing U.S. wholesale prices to prices in other countries and other drugs, as the bill requires, is a blunt yardstick — different countries use different pricing systems, and a drug's value can diverge from its cost of manufacture [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit would have been direct and large — government review of every drug price, public price information, and real leverage through patent revocation — while the main cost is a plausible but slower-moving one: less incentive to develop new drugs. The patent-revocation remedy was a blunt instrument that courts and manufacturers would likely have contested for years, so the bill's bark might have exceeded its bite. Still, this was one of the strongest price-control proposals for prescription drugs of its era.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee in April 1993, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Durbin introduced the Prescription Drug Consumer Protection Act on March 23, 1993, with 17 cosponsors [S1] [S4] [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on March 23, 1993 [S5].
On April 14, 1993, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, and the action record ends there [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or a hearing on the record, and expired when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off: no government board ever reviewed their prices and no drug ever faced patent revocation for price. Consumers are left with the same prescription prices and no federal consumer's guide to drug pricing.

for.name: Rep. Richard J. Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on March 23, 1993.

for.name: 17 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors in support of the bill.

against.name: Rep. John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee; he never brought it to a committee markup or vote, and it died there.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: The industry opposed government drug price controls during the 1993-94 health care debate, the policy fight this bill was part of.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Democrats or allied Independents, and the bill stalled entirely within a House run by the Democratic majority; no Republican support is recorded.

industries.note: Their prices would face government review with mandatory data disclosures, and refusing to cut an 'excessive' price could cost them a patent — the monopoly that sustains their pricing. Their interest ran directly against consumers' interest in lower drug prices.
A revoked patent would let generic manufacturers legally copy the drug and compete on price, and consumers would benefit from that competition at the same time.

The bill ordered a study of how drugmakers charge hospitals, mail-order pharmacies, and HMOs much less than wholesalers — a price disparity that squeezes local pharmacies; the study was framed as protecting consumers.
